Cosmic Eye

  1. Pick a target in the Library on the left. Each card shows which bands it has real data for, and Spectrum if it has a visible-light spectrum.
  2. Read the spectrum in the middle. It is the target's real recorded light, spread out by your disperser. Dark lines are light that was absorbed; bright lines are light that was emitted. Every line carries its wavelength in nm.
  3. Match a line: drag its ? tag onto a row of the Reference chart (or tap the tag, then tap a row). The row shows its nearest line and the gap Δ. Within 0.6 nm (1.5 nm for molecule bands) the line locks and gets its element.
  4. Tap a row in the Reference chart (with no line picked) to lay its lines over the spectrum for a quick comparison. Tap it again to remove them.
  5. Zoom with + / −, the mouse wheel, or the keys + and −. When zoomed, drag the spectrum sideways, or use the Overview strip below it: tap a spot to jump there (it zooms in ×4 if you are not zoomed yet) and drag the gold window to move. Fit shows all of it again.
  6. Switch Prism / Grating and try each material: the same light is redrawn through each one.
  7. Turn the waveband dial (drag or tap) to see the target in radio, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray or gamma rays, using real telescope images.
  8. When you are ready, press Mystery test: you get an unlabeled spectrum, match its lines, then say what it is made of and what kind of object it is.
  9. End session shows your session report. Import photo (optional) puts a picture of your own diffraction pattern beside the reference lines.

Keys: ← → turn the dial · + − zoom · 0 fit · P prism/grating · Esc closes pop-ups.

Class 8–11 · CBSE/NCERT Science & Physics · Light, atoms and stars

By the end you should be able to:

  1. Explain where spectral lines come from: the source makes them. A prism or grating only spreads the light out; it never adds or removes lines.
  2. Match a line to an element by its wavelength in nm, using a reference chart, without relying on colour.
  3. Describe what a Fraunhofer line is: an atom absorbs exactly the photon energy (E = hf = hc/λ) that lifts one of its electrons between two allowed levels.
  4. Explain why one object looks completely different in radio, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma rays: each band shows different matter at different temperatures.
  5. Explain that visible light is a sliver of the electromagnetic spectrum, about 2% of the dial from radio to gamma.
  6. Read an unlabeled spectrum: say what it is made of and what kind of object produced it.

The physics used

E = hf = hc/λ  ·  d sinθ = mλ  ·  n(λ) = A + B/λ²

Grating: d is the line spacing, m the order. A grating spreads light almost evenly in wavelength and gives several orders. Prism: glass bends blue more than red (n is larger for short λ), giving one narrow spread that squeezes the red end. Real Fraunhofer wavelengths (air, nm): Ca II K 393.37 and H 396.85, Hβ 486.13, Na D 588.995 and 589.592, Hα 656.28; the 21 cm hydrogen line is 1420.4 MHz.

Teacher note. All data is real and bundled, so the tool runs offline. The solar spectrum is the Kitt Peak FTS flux atlas (continuum-normalised); its overall slope is drawn with a 5772 K blackbody. Star and galaxy spectra are SDSS spectra (resolution about 0.3 nm, resampled here to 0.1 nm per point), shifted to their rest frame using the survey's measured velocity, so line wavelengths can be compared directly with the lab values. The sodium D pair is only 0.6 nm apart, so in the SDSS red dwarf it shows as one broad dip near 589.0 nm; the much sharper solar atlas splits it in two (zoom in). Telescope images are false-colour: each band is invisible to our eyes, so colour is assigned. Prism uses 60° BK7 glass at minimum deviation.

Data credits

  • Solar spectrum: Kitt Peak National Observatory FTS solar flux atlas, R. L. Kurucz (2005), NSO/NOAO.
  • Star and galaxy spectra and sky images: Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS DR17/DR18).
  • Crab Nebula, five bands: NASA, ESA, G. Dubner (IAFE, CONICET-University of Buenos Aires) et al.; A. Loll et al.; T. Temim et al.; F. Seward et al.; VLA/NRAO/AUI/NSF; Chandra/CXC; Spitzer/JPL-Caltech; XMM-Newton/ESA; Hubble/STScI (NASA PIA21474).
  • Gamma-ray sky: NASA/DOE/Fermi LAT Collaboration; NASA SVS/F. Reddy.
  • Sun images: NASA/SDO and the AIA and HMI science teams.
  • 21 cm sky: HI4PI, Parkes Radio Telescope/100-m Effelsberg/CSIRO/MPIfR (CC BY 4.0, via NOIRLab).
  • Infrared sky: NASA/GSFC COBE DIRBE. Visible Milky Way: ESO/S. Brunier (CC BY 4.0).
